pages.text: Graphical abstract e This programme is a staged path from concepts to reusable scientific outputs. The aim is not to accumulate disconnected topics, but to learn how explanation, computation, uncertainty, validation, and software practice combine into defensible research work. Figure 1: A compact graphical abstract. The figure keeps only the four main stages of the programme: core concepts, method building, cumulative projects, and reusable research outputs. Research software, reproducibility, and documentation run through the entire sequence rather than appearing at the end. ii

pages.label: front matter
pages.text: The big picture: one evidence loop e The whole book is organized around one recurring question: what would make a computational scientific claim defensible? A claim is defensible only if the scientific question, the representation, the computation, the evidence, the uncertainty analysis, and the final decision all remain visible. None of these layers can substitute for the others. This is why the book does not treat AI as an isolated add-on and does not hide software engineering in an appendix. A neural surrogate can change the meaning of mechanistic parameters; an observation model can determine practical identifiability; a discretization can create or suppress dynamics; a software interface can silently change units. The evidence loop is therefore both a scientific workflow and a curriculum map. Figure 2: The evidence loop in one page. Start by defining the scientific question, build a representation, compute predictions, compare with evidence, assess uncertainty, then decide and revise. Good scientific software supports every stage of the loop. iii

pages.text: iv / 342 How this edition is supposed to teach The standard for this edition is not “mention the topic” but “help the reader do the analysis.” For each major concept, you should be able to locate most of the following moves in the surrounding text, examples, e figures, code, or exercises. 1. Plain-language definition: what the concept is in ordinary scientific language. 2. Why it matters: what failure or question makes the concept necessary. 3. Minimal example: a small case simple enough to inspect directly. 4. Formal statement: the equation, algorithm, or object used in practice. 5. Worked reasoning: the calculation or logic carried out step by step. 6. Code connection: where the mathematics becomes computation. 7. Interpretation: what the output means scientifically. 8. Failure mode: the common way the concept is misused or overclaimed. 9. Transfer: how the same idea enters a project or research artifact. If a section feels too compressed, use this list diagnostically: ask which of the nine moves is missing. The front-matter glossary below is intended to reduce the burden of remembering unstated background while reading later chapters. A quick glossary before the chapters Term Plain-language definition and why it matters Model A controlled abstraction of a real system, built for a specific question. A model is not reality in miniature; it is a simplification whose assumptions must stay visible. State variable A quantity the model evolves internally, such as biomass, concentration, or volt- age. States are often not observed directly. Parameter A quantity that controls the behaviour of the model without being updated by the model dynamics, such as a rate constant or elastic modulus. Observable A measured quantity or derived output connected to the internal state by an observation function. Confusing states with observables is a major source of false confidence. Inverse problem The task of inferring unknown states, parameters, inputs, or structure from obser- vations. Most model fitting is an inverse problem. Identifiability The question of whether the available data can uniquely constrain the unknown quantities. A parameter can be numerically estimated without being scientifically identifiable. Conditioning The sensitivity of the mathematical answer to small perturbations in the in- puts. Poor conditioning means tiny errors in data or coefficients can cause large changes in the inferred answer. Regularization An explicit way to stabilize or constrain an inverse problem when the data do not support every direction equally. It is not just a numerical trick; it changes the information geometry of the problem. Prior / posterior In Bayesian inference, the prior encodes assumptions before seeing current data, while the posterior updates those assumptions after combining them with the likelihood from observed data. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

pages.label: front matter
pages.text: v / 342 Uncertainty propaga- The step where uncertainty in parameters, states, or inputs is pushed forward tion to the scientific quantity of interest. Decision-relevant uncertainty lives in the outputs, not only in parameter tables. Validation The process of checking whether a model or learned system is adequate for its intended scientific use. Validation is broader than goodness of fit. e Reproducibility The ability for another person or future you to rerun, inspect, and verify the com- putational chain. Reproducibility supports trust but does not, by itself, prove scientific correctness. How to work through the book Read actively. For a new method, first identify the scientific question and the minimal example. Then follow the derivation, inspect the figure, run or adapt the code, and finish by stating what evidence would falsify the method on a real problem. Problems are collected at the ends of chapters so that explanation remains readable. External resources are used as active studios: when a chapter points to BioModels, PEtab, SALib, PyMC, SciML, BEIR or The Turing Way, the task is to reproduce, inspect, modify, or evaluate something specific rather than merely browse a link. The course uses three levels of evidence repeatedly. First, verify a method on a case where the answer or qualitative behavior is known. Second, move to a community benchmark where implementations can be compared. Third, move to a real scientific dataset or model where the ground truth is incomplete and model criticism becomes part of the work. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

pages.text: Research continuity and the October ap- e pointment This programme is prepared for an experienced mechanistic modeller, not a beginner restarting from Python syntax. Build four completed investigations attached to existing work rather than creating four unrelated flagship repositories. Numerical trust can strengthen the fatty-acid bistability analysis; observation design and identifiability can strengthen fatty-acid synthesis; multiscale inference and selective ML can strengthen photosynthesis; stochastic assumptions can be tested through the T-cell models. FokoLab provides the delivery and independent-usability investigation. These links are now operational learning contracts in research_pathways/. They do not assert that the original repositories were edited, that their results were independently validated here, or that the coming postdoc has a specified work package. Preserve collaborators’ attribution, including Yvonne Danisch’s acknowledged computational contribution in the photosynthesis work. Define the scientific question before allocating the year The planning scenario is the reported October-start, one-year appointment. Agree the primary question, expected research output, model/data access, collaborators, public-release permissions and protected learning time with the supervisors. A 50% appointment does not imply that the rest of the week is freely available for training. An illustrative capacity budget is six protected hours per week over forty active weeks: 240 hours. Within that budget, favour one primary scientific result and one maintainable workflow. An ML extension must outperform an appropriate baseline on a relevant scientific objective or produce a defensible negative result. An agent is optional; a deterministic API may be the better implementation. vi

Machine Learning A–Z [2026]: ML, DL, AI with AWS, Python & R (Kirill Eremenko, Hadelin de Ponteves and collaborators) provides a broad implementation and cloud track through classical super- vised/unsupervised ML, model selection and boosting, ANN/CNN material, dimensionality reduction, and an extensive AWS path covering preprocessing, SageMaker model development, deployment targets, CI/CD, monitoring, model cards and cost/operations. The book deliberately goes deeper where these courses are broad: numerical conditioning and solver trust; mechanistic modelling and observation operators; identifiability and profile likelihood; Bayesian workflow and simulation-based inference; sensitivity/OED; multiscale modelling; scientific ML and learned-closure confounding; equation discovery; leakage-safe biological validation; evidence-grounded retrieval/agents; and scientific-software verification. Dependencies remain explicit: scientific representation and numerical verification precede inference; scientific Python supports every executable layer; observation and validation design precede ML; repro- ducible software accompanies every stage. The programme should therefore complement the courses rather than replay them. The four evidence gates Gate A (after verified baseline): verified numerical computation. You can explain conditioning, reproduce solver convergence evidence, and package a small numerical component with tests. Gate B (after inference diagnostics): defensible inference. You can distinguish fit from identifiability, construct a PEtab-style data contract, quantify uncertainty, and explain which experiment would reduce ambiguity. Gate C (after held-out comparison): validated learning. You can design leakage-safe real-data validation, differentiate through a simulator, and test a hybrid model outside its training regime. Release (after independent reproduction): evidence-aware scientific product. At least one portfolio repository can be cloned, tested, executed, inspected, and defended without relying on undocumented local state. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

pages.text: How examples, exercises, hints, and solu- e tions work in this edition The intended learning progression is worked reasoning, a guided investigation, staged hints, a reference comparison and a project artifact. These are distinct evidence levels. Appendix A provides 44 guided resolutions; not every guide is a fully closed computational investigation. The four tumour reference notebooks and their results now form one completed, bounded synthetic chain, reproduced in Chapter 26. Other supplied examples are labeled by their demonstrated scope rather than by the amount of advice they contain. Use learner templates before opening the reference. A template that raises NotImplementedError is intentionally unfinished; a passing import test is not evidence that its scientific exercise has been solved. Each main learner project now includes executable acceptance checks and domain-specific interfaces in exercise.py. x

pages.text: How the learning system works e This edition retains the strongest correction from earlier iterations: it removes the pattern in which “deep pedagogy” was appended after a chapter had already finished teaching the topic. Each cumulative thread is now inserted next to the method it exercises. Work in the order: predict →derive →compute →diagnose →transfer to the project. Hints are progressive. The worked resolutions in Appendix A are intended to be opened only after you have produced a diagnostic artifact of your own. The design is intentionally benchmark-first where a maintained benchmark exists: verify a numerical method on a case with known behavior, move to a community benchmark, then transfer the method to a scientific case whose ground truth is incomplete. This mirrors the problem-set/solution culture of graduate numerical-methods teaching and the workflow emphasis in maintained scientific-computing ecosystems. xii

CHAPTER 1 C Scientific Models as Executable Arguments ◎Learning objectives • scientific contracts • observation/noise separation • limiting-case verification Make the learner treat a model as an executable scientific argument rather ☼Pedagogical than a collection of equations. objective MultiScaleTwin / TumorTherapyTwin: model contract, observables, invari- ¨ Project link ant tests. Scientific modelling is treated as evidence engineering: representation, observation, computation, and software are separate but coupled layers. 1.1 A model is an executable scientific argument The central object in this book is not an equation, an estimator, a neural network, or a software package. It is a scientific claim whose chain of support can be inspected. A model states which entities exist, how they interact, which quantities are observed, which processes are ignored, and under what conditions its predictions should be trusted. Computation then turns those commitments into consequences. Data confront those consequences. Software preserves the chain well enough that another person can inspect it. This framing changes how we read every later chapter. A good fit is not automatically good evidence. A converged solver is not automatically a correct discretization. A calibrated classifier is not automatically transportable. A reproducible repository is not automatically scientifically valid. Each layer has a different failure mode, and the job of the computational scientist is to keep them separated long enough to diagnose them. 1.1.1 Study a real curation workflow before writing your own model The BioModels training material is a useful model of what “model correctness” means in practice. BioModels distinguishes literature-derived mechanistic models from automatically generated resources and describes curation as checking the encoded structure against the publication, verifying parameters and units, and reproducing published behavior with an independent simulator. See https://www. ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/biomodels-quick-tour/ and the BioModels FAQ at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biomodels/faq. 2

Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 3 / 342 Do not merely browse the site. Choose one curated model and reconstruct a one-page scientific contract: biological scope, state variables, parameters, observables, units, initial conditions, interventions, and the exact published behavior that curation reproduces. Then identify at least three claims that the SBML file cannot establish by itself. This exercise establishes the standard used throughout the book: C representation, evidence, and computation are distinct objects. 1.2 A model is a controlled abstraction A mechanistic model is not a miniature copy of reality. It is a deliberately simplified causal representation built for a question. The same biological system can require different models depending on whether the objective is explanation, prediction, parameter inference, control, extrapolation, or experimental design. A useful modelling statement has five parts: system + scale + question + assumptions + observables. (1.1) For example, “model photosynthesis” is underspecified. A stronger formulation is: predict leaf carbon assimilation over minute-to-hour environmental variation using biochemical and stomatal processes, assuming spatially homogeneous leaf properties and quasi-steady intracellular intermediates, with gas-exchange measurements as observables. The formulation determines which mechanisms belong in the model. 1.2.1 Mechanistic versus phenomenological A mechanistic component aims to represent a process through hypothesized causal structure. A phenomenological component represents an empirical relationship without necessarily claiming the underlying mechanism. The distinction is not binary. The Michaelis–Menten form VmaxS v(S) = (1.2) Km + S can be mechanistically derived under specific assumptions, yet it is also frequently used phenomenologically when those assumptions are not verified. Therefore, ask not only “is this equation mechanistic?” but: • Which variables have physical/biological meaning? • Which relationships arise from conservation or known kinetics? • Which terms are closures or empirical approximations? • Which assumptions are required for the derivation? • Which parameters can be transferred outside the calibration context? 1.2.2 State variables and observables are different Let the latent mechanistic state be x(t) and measured data be y(t). A general state-space formulation is ˙x = f(x, u, p, t), (1.3) y = h(x, p) + ϵ. (1.4) Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 4 / 342 The observation function h matters. Experiments rarely measure every model state directly. Ignoring the measurement process can create false identifiability. Two internal states may influence the same observable combination, making them impossible to infer separately even if the ODE solution itself C is unique. 1.3 Conservation laws before equations A strong modelling habit is to start from balances. For an amount X in a compartment, dX = inflows −outflows + production −consumption. (1.5) dt This structure prevents many sign and bookkeeping errors. For a concentration c = X/V , changing volume introduces additional terms: dc 1 dX dV = −X . (1.6) dt V dt V 2 dt Treating concentration dynamics as amount dynamics without accounting for volume change can be scientifically wrong. 1.3.1 Dimensions as an error detector Every additive term in an equation must have the same physical dimensions. If dx = k1x −k2xy, (1.7) dt then the dimensions of k1 and k2 must make both right-hand terms have dimension [x]/[t]. Dimensional analysis cannot prove a model correct, but it can prove many equations wrong. 1.3.2 Nondimensionalization reveals structure Suppose ˙X = aX −bXY, (1.8) ˙Y = cXY −dY. Chapter 1. Scientific Models as Executable Arguments 5 / 342 1.3.3 Timescales A process with rate constant k has characteristic timescale roughly τ ∼1 (1.12) C k. If one process acts on milliseconds and another on hours, treating them identically can create stiffness and may suggest model reduction. If τfast ≪τslow, a fast variable may approximately satisfy a quasi-steady relation. But the approximation needs justification; transients or perturbations can invalidate it. 1.3.4 Scale is more than spatial size Multiscale systems can involve different: • spatial scales; • temporal scales; • organizational scales; • modelling representations; • data resolutions. A molecular event, cell response, tissue transport process, organism phenotype, and environmental driver can have qualitatively different state representations. Multiscale modelling is therefore not “one huge ODE.” It is the principled coupling of representations whose assumptions may differ. 1.3.5 Where ML belongs Machine learning is most valuable when it addresses a specific limitation. Typical roles include: 1. surrogate: approximate an expensive mechanistic simulator; 2. closure: learn an unresolved process or scale coupling; 3. observation model: map high-dimensional measurements to mechanistic states; 4. inference accelerator: amortize parameter or state estimation; 5. representation learning: compress complex data while retaining predictive structure; 6. model discrepancy: represent systematic mismatch between mechanistic prediction and data; 7. experimental policy: choose informative experiments or simulations. We revisit linear algebra through observability, conditioning, inverse problems, and regularization rather than elementary matrix manipulation. 2.1 Information geometry rather than matrix manipulation For an expert modeller, the reason to revisit linear algebra is not to relearn matrix multiplication. It is to see how information is amplified, discarded, or rendered non-identifiable by a map. Singular vectors expose combinations of parameters or states that the data can and cannot see. Conditioning measures the sensitivity of an answer to perturbations in that information. Regularization is therefore not a numerical trick appended after failure; it is an explicit decision about which poorly observed directions will be suppressed. The chapter’s recurring question is: which directions in the domain are supported by the evidence, and which are being created by the algorithm or prior assumptions? Keep that question when the matrices later become Jacobians, Fisher-information matrices, kernel matrices, or neural tangent approximations. Linear algebra is the language in which most computational science is secretly written. A local sensitivity matrix tells which combinations of parameters the experiment can see. Newton’s method solves a linearized system. A discretized PDE is a sparse matrix equation. Kalman filters propagate covariance matrices. PCA searches for informative subspaces. Ridge regression modifies the spectrum of an inverse problem. Neural-network layers are learned affine maps. If matrices remain “arrays of coefficients,” these topics appear unrelated and memorization becomes fragile. If you understand spaces, projections, spectra and conditioning, the later methods reuse the same geometry. 12

Its coordinates depend on a basis. This distinction matters in scientific models because changing coordinates can change numerical conditioning without changing the underlying physical state. A physiological state might be represented by concentrations ci, log- C concentrations zi = log ci, or dimensionless deviations (ci −c⋆i )/c⋆i . The three coordinate systems encode the same phenomenon differently, but optimization and inference can behave very differently. For x ∈Rn, common norms are ∥x∥1 = X |xi|, ∥x∥2 = (xT x)1/2, ∥x∥∞= max |xi|. i i A weighted quadratic norm ∥x∥2W = xT Wx, with positive-definite W, can encode uncertainty, physical units or scientific importance. This is not cosmetic: changing the norm changes what “close” means. Worked analysis: 1: scaling changes the scientific objective Suppose a model predicts core temperature T and plasma concentration C. The residual is r = (Tpred −Tobs, Cpred −Cobs) = (0.4, 0.8). Raw least squares gives contributions 0.16 and 0.64, suggesting concentration dominates. If measurement standard deviations are (0.2, 1.0), the standardized residual is (2, 0.8), with contributions 4 and 0.64. The correct weighted least-squares objective is J = rT Σ−1r, where Σ is the observation-error covariance. The algebraic operation is matrix multiplication; the scientific interpretation is that deviations are measured in units of expected noise. An optimizer cannot decide this scaling for you. 2.2 Matrices as maps A matrix A ∈Rm×n represents a linear map A : Rn →Rm, x 7→Ax. The jth column is the output produced by the jth input basis vector. The column space C(A) is the set of attainable outputs. The null space N(A) = {x : Ax = 0} contains input perturbations that the map cannot see. Rank is the dimension of the attainable output space. C If rk = 0, the equation is satisfied. Therefore a good iterative method should reduce a scientifically meaningful residual, not merely report a change in iterates. Chapter 3. Krylov Solvers, Sparse Systems, and Numerical Evidence 31 / 342 3.5 GMRES: minimize the residual in the Krylov space GMRES chooses xk = x0 + Qky C to minimize ∥b −Axk∥2 . Using Arnoldi, rk = r0 −AQky = ∥r0∥q1 −Qk+1 ¯Hky. Because Qk+1 has orthonormal columns, ∥rk∥2 = ∥r0∥e1 −¯Hky 2 . So each GMRES step solves a tiny least-squares problem. This derivation connects Chapter 2’s projection geometry directly to a large sparse solver. Interpretation: GMRES is “best residual so far” in an expanding information space. At iteration k, the algorithm knows only what can be constructed from r0, Ar0, . . . , Ak−1r0. Within that information budget, GMRES selects the correction that minimizes the Euclidean residual. This explains both its robustness and its memory cost: retaining a growing orthonormal basis is expensive, so restarted GMRES trades memory for possible loss of convergence information. 3.6 Preconditioning: solve an equivalent but easier problem A preconditioner M ≈A should be cheap to apply and make the transformed system better conditioned or spectrally clustered. A diagonal Jacobi preconditioner uses M = diag(A). Incomplete LU/Cholesky, algebraic multigrid and physics-based block preconditioners can be far stronger. The right choice exploits structure; there is no universal “best preconditioner.” Failure to watch: A small residual in the wrong norm. The jth column tells how all outputs change when input xj changes. The ith row is the gradient of output component fi. For scalar f : Rn →R, the Jacobian is represented by the gradient ∇f. The second-order Taylor expansion is 1 f(x + h) ≈f(x) + ∇f(x)T h + 2hT H(x)h, where H is the Hessian. Interpretation: Gradient versus Hessian. The gradient is a local slope vector: it identifies the direction of greatest first-order increase. The Hessian describes how that slope changes and therefore encodes local curvature. Optimization methods use the gradient to know which way to move and curvature to know how far and how directions interact. 4.1.2 Directional derivatives and JVPs The directional derivative along v is Dvf(x) = Jf(x)v. This Jacobian-vector product (JVP) computes how outputs change under one input perturbation direction without forming the full Jacobian. For a simulator with millions of states, Jv can be feasible even when J is impossible to store. A vector-Jacobian product (VJP) is wT Jf(x), or equivalently Jf(x)T w as a column. Reverse-mode autodiff/backprop efficiently computes VJPs. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Scientific software can return smooth plots while solving the equations inaccurately. Numerical analysis supplies the discipline for separating “the code ran” from “the numerical approximation is trustworthy.” This is increasingly important when simulations become training data for ML or are embedded inside optimization: solver bias can be learned, optimized and confidently deployed. Four error layers. Keep these separate: 1. model-form error: equations omit or misrepresent reality; 2. parameter/data uncertainty: inputs are imperfectly known; 46

C 5.2 Consistency, stability and convergence For a time-stepping method, local truncation error measures how well one exact solution step satisfies the discrete formula. Consistency means truncation error vanishes as step size goes to zero. Stability means perturbations are not amplified uncontrollably. Under appropriate conditions, consistency plus stability gives convergence. Euler method. For ˙y = f(t, y), yn+1 = yn + hf(tn, yn). Taylor expansion of the exact solution gives 1 y(t + h) = y(t) + hy′(t) + 2h2y′′(ξ), so the local error is O(h2) and accumulated global error is O(h). Runge–Kutta idea. Higher-order RK methods combine several slope evaluations to match more Taylor terms without explicitly computing high derivatives. The ubiquitous RK4 is fourth order for sufficiently smooth problems, but adaptive embedded methods are generally preferable in scientific production because they estimate local error and vary step size. 5.2.1 Absolute stability and stiffness Apply a method to the test equation y′ = λy. A one-step method produces yn+1 = R(hλ)yn. Stability requires |R(hλ)| ≤1 for decaying modes. Explicit Euler has R(z) = 1 + z, so for real negative λ it requires −2 < hλ < 0. A fast decaying mode with large |λ| can force tiny steps even if the scientific behavior of interest evolves slowly. This is stiffness. Interpretation: Stiffness is a numerical time-scale mismatch. A stiff system contains stable fast modes that the solution may quickly settle onto, but explicit methods must still take small steps to avoid numerical instability. Implicit methods spend more work per step solving nonlinear/linear systems, but can take much larger stable steps. 5.2.2 Choosing ODE solvers A solver choice should follow the equation class and the evidence requirement, not habit. These are different stochastic processes and can yield different equilibria, front speeds, cluster patterns, and correlations. 15.4.1 A minimal SIS ABM Worked microcase: scheduling changes an outcome Consider three agents in a line, A −B −C. At the beginning of a nominal step only A is infected. The rule is deterministic for this microcase: an infected agent transmits to a susceptible neighbor when that contact is processed. Under a synchronous update, all contacts read the state at the beginning of the step. A can infect B, but B was susceptible at the read phase and cannot infect C until the next step. The end state is therefore (I, I, S). Under a random-sequential order A →B →C, B becomes infected immediately and can infect C in the same nominal step, giving (I, I, I). A minimal model is ∂c ∂2c c = D −q(c; Vmax, Km), q(c) = Vmax ∂t ∂x2 Km + c. At the vascular boundary c(0, t) = cb(t); at x = L use zero flux cx(L, t) = 0 as a symmetry/impermeable approximation. This boundary choice is a scientific assumption and must be defended for the geometry being represented. Assumption audit: model scope. The slab ignores heterogeneous vasculature, cell-level variation, advection, and changing tissue geometry. It is appropriate for learning how oxygen profiles depend on diffusion/consumption and for testing inference/experimental design. It should not be sold as a patient-specific tumor model without additional evidence. 26.2.1 Nondimensionalization Choose ˜x = x/L, ˜c = c/cb, and diffusion time τD = L2/D. In the low-concentration linearized regime q ≈ (Vmax/Km)c, the steady equation becomes d2˜c VmaxL2 −ϕ2˜c = 0, ϕ2 = . d˜x2 DKm The Thiele-like modulus ϕ shows immediately that steady oxygen profiles may identify only combinations of Vmax, D, Km, and L without independent information. Compare three designs: 1. steady profile only; 2. transient profile after a step change in cb; 3. steady + transient with an independent measurement of D. Estimate (D, Vmax, Km) and compute sensitivity matrices. The singular vectors should reveal that the steady-only design is weakest in parameter combinations preserving the dimensionless consumption/diffusion ratio. Worked analysis - C1-W2: profile likelihood changes with experiment. In a steady-only design, profile D while reoptimizing consumption parameters. Expect a broad valley. Add transient observations: changing D alters time scale and the profile should sharpen. Add independent D: the remaining uptake parameters can separate further if concentration spans both c ≪Km and c ≳Km regimes. 26.2.4 Experimental design Candidate measurement depths and times have sensitivity vectors. A design concentrated near the boundary may estimate cb well but contain little information about deep consumption. Choose measurements to increase the smallest information eigenvalue. Compare this OED design with equally spaced measurements using parameter-recovery simulation. 26.2.5 Uncertainty and decision quantity A plausible decision quantity is hypoxic fraction/region, e.g. length of tissue with c < ccrit. Propagate parameter/posterior uncertainty to this derived quantity. Chapter 26. Integrated Scientific Cases: From Evidence to Decision 298 / 342 hydraulics, energy balance, climate forcing, and adaptation. It deliberately exposes identifiability and hybrid-model confounding that do not appear in a single-equation toy model. Ç 26.3 System decomposition Represent net assimilation A as a biochemical demand constrained by CO2 supply. A generic C3 formulation uses the minimum of Rubisco-limited and electron-transport-limited rates, with temperature- dependent kinetic terms. Stomatal conductance gs controls CO2 diffusion and water loss. Leaf tempera- ture Tl emerges from an energy balance rather than being assigned equal to air temperature. Hydraulic state constrains stomatal behavior under water deficit. Assumption audit: avoid hidden algebraic loops. If assimilation depends on intercellular CO2, which depends on stomatal conductance, while stomatal conductance depends on assimilation, the model contains an algebraic coupling. Make the solve explicit: formulate a root/DAE problem or a consistent nested iteration with convergence checks. Silent fixed-point iteration is part of the numerical method and must be documented. 26.3.1 A minimal coupled formulation Use A = Fbio(Ci, Tl, θb), A = gc(Ca −Ci), with gc related to gs, and transpiration E = gw VPD(Tl, RH). A simplified leaf energy balance is Rn = H(Tl −Ta) + λE. Hydraulics may impose E = (ψs −ψl)/Rh or a more detailed conductance relation. The coupled solve links biochemical, diffusive, thermal, and hydraulic scales. Worked analysis - C2-W1: why fixing leaf temperature can bias inference. Suppose a high- radiation treatment raises Tl several degrees above Ta. If the model fixes Tl = Ta, the temperature dependence of biochemical parameters is evaluated too low. The optimizer can compensate by changing Vc max or stomatal parameters. A good fit does not imply correct physiology; the missing energy balance creates structured parameter bias. 26.3.2 Identifiability by intervention Gas-exchange data at one light/CO2/temperature condition can leave biochemical and stomatal parame- ters correlated. Varying CO2 targets biochemical limitation; light response separates electron-transport limitation; VPD/water potential informs stomatal/hydraulic components; thermal perturbation informs energy/kinetic responses. The experiment should be designed around parameter-direction separation. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Chapter 26. Integrated Scientific Cases: From Evidence to Decision 299 / 342 26.3.3 Multiobjective adaptation A plant strategy is not naturally a scalar objective. Consider max{Atotal, −Wuse, −Tstress} Ç under hydraulic safety and trait bounds. Generate Pareto fronts rather than choosing an arbitrary weighted sum first. Compare climate scenarios and identify which traits shift with environment. Worked analysis - C2-W2: Pareto front under water stress. Under moist conditions, high stomatal conductance may increase assimilation with modest water penalty. Under high VPD/limited soil water, the same trait moves the system toward hydraulic constraints. A single “optimal stomatal conductance” across climates is therefore a category error unless the objective and environment are fixed. 26.3.4 Robust optimization Climate forcing and parameters are uncertain. Compare nominal optimization against a robust objective such as expected assimilation with a chance constraint on hydraulic safety. Evaluate on held-out climate draws, including extremes not used during optimization. 26.3.5 Hybrid Scientific ML closure Suppose residuals show a condition-dependent bias in stomatal response. A neural closure gϕ can be added, but constrain its role. Train on some climates and evaluate on held-out climates/interventions. Compare mechanistic parameter recovery with and without closure. Plot closure magnitude against the state variables to see whether it is learning a plausible missing process or merely canceling mechanistic terms. Failure to watch: hybrid success by compensation. If the closure is expressive enough, it can make the simulator fit every training climate while destroying the interpretability of physiological parameters. The primary hybrid evidence is not training RMSE; it is improved residual structure plus preserved parameter meaning and improved held-out intervention prediction. Case exercises. Chapter 26. Integrated Scientific Cases: From Evidence to Decision 300 / 342 Worked analysis - C3-W1: same mean, different noise. Two parameter sets can produce the same steady protein mean while changing burst size and variance. If only population-average protein is measured, they can be hard to distinguish. Single-cell distribution or time-correlation information can separate them. This is identifiability through richer observations, not a better optimizer. For the two-stage model, compare simulated moments with known/derived moment equations or a high-accuracy reference. 26.4.2 Observation model Microscopy may observe fluorescence y = aP + b + ϵ, possibly with shot noise, background, saturation, and segmentation error. The observation model can dominate low-copy measurements. Calibrating a, b or including controls can be more informative than adding simulator complexity. 26.4.3 State-space inference If measurements are time-lapse but protein/mRNA are partially observed, filtering/smoothing can infer hidden trajectories. Innovations should reveal whether a Gaussian filter approximation is adequate. At low counts, particle filtering may better represent skewed/discrete uncertainty. 26.4.4 SBI formulation When the full observation pipeline includes stochastic simulation, nonlinear image summaries, censoring, or other intractable components, define a simulator from θ to summary/features x. Worked analysis - C3-W2: summary statistic destroys identifiability. If the simulator output is compressed to mean protein only, parameter combinations controlling burst frequency and burst size can remain confounded. Adding variance and autocorrelation or full distributional embeddings can restore information. SBI cannot recover information removed by the summary. 26.4.5 Simulation-based calibration Draw θ(r) from the prior, simulate x(r), infer posterior, and evaluate the rank of the true parameter among posterior draws. Across repetitions, ranks should be approximately uniform for a calibrated procedure under the assumed generative model. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

Chapter 26. Integrated Scientific Cases: From Evidence to Decision 301 / 342 26.5 PK model Use a two-compartment amount model from Module 3. Observed central concentration is C = Ac/Vc. A pharmacodynamic effect can be Ç EmaxC E(C) = E0 − EC50 + C or another monotone/saturating relation depending on the application. 26.5.1 Sparse-sampling identifiability Early samples primarily inform distribution; late samples inform terminal elimination. If sampling misses one phase, Q, Vp, CL, Vc can be correlated. Use sensitivity/time-course analysis before fitting. Worked analysis - C4-W1: dose-normalized curve is not enough. Two patients can have similar concentration curves over a short window through compensation between volume and clearance but very different extrapolated exposure. A fit restricted to early data can therefore predict later AUC poorly. Hold out the terminal phase or use external priors/hierarchical information. 26.5.2 Hierarchical population model For patient i, a positive parameter can be log CLi = log CLpop + βw log(wi/w0) + ηi, ηi ∼N(0, ω2). This borrows strength while preserving individual variability. Validate the population model with posterior predictive distributions stratified by covariates and patient-level residuals. 26.5.3 Dose optimization under uncertainty Define target exposure range or effect and safety constraints. A nominal dose based on posterior mean parameters can be fragile. Evaluate dose choices across posterior draws and optimize expected utility or chance constraints. Worked analysis - C4-W2: posterior uncertainty changes dose. If a patient’s clearance posterior has a long low-clearance tail, the mean-optimal dose may carry substantial overdose probability. A risk-sensitive policy can reduce dose or request another measurement. Uncertainty therefore changes the decision, not only the error bar. 26.5.4 MPC and therapeutic drug monitoring At each measurement, update latent state/individual parameters, solve a finite-horizon dose problem, apply the first action, and repeat. The controller should suspend or fall back when state-estimation diagnostics indicate mismatch or measurements are outside the model’s scope. 26.6 Prediction question Use a longitudinal molecular dataset such as GEO GSE91061 or another public study with repeated samples per subject. All preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, feature selection, and calibration occur within training folds. Report score distributions and patient counts. Worked analysis - C5-W1: batch signal beats biology. Suppose response labels are imbalanced across sequencing batches. A model achieves high CV performance under random sample splitting because batch signatures correlate with outcome. The language model should not invent numerical metrics. Every generated claim that depends on the local corpus should be linked to retrieved evidence or marked unsupported. If the corpus contains conflicting studies on a pathway, the correct behavior is to retrieve both, state the conflict, and identify differences in cohort/design rather than synthesize an artificial consensus. For each case, build an evidence graph with five columns: representation, observations, numerical computation, inferential or learning claim, and decision. Draw an arrow only when you can name the assumption that justifies it. Then mark every arrow that has been independently verified or validated. The empty cells are often more informative than the filled ones. Case synthesis 1: tissue oxygen transport. Start from a conservation law for oxygen in tissue, choose boundary conditions, discretize, and verify spatial convergence on a manufactured solution. Only after the forward solver is trusted should you ask which diffusion and consumption parameters can be inferred from sparse oxygen measurements. Compare the sensitivity singular vectors with the spatial locations of sensors. If the weak direction corresponds to a trade-off between diffusivity and consumption, propose a sensor placement or perturbation that separates them. The final claim is not “the optimizer found D and q.” It is “under these boundary conditions and measurement locations, this parameter combination is supported to this uncertainty.” Case synthesis 2: carbon–water–heat physiology. The model couples photosynthetic carbon gain, stomatal or hydraulic regulation, and leaf temperature. Begin by defining the coupling variables and time scales rather than assembling equations ad hoc. Quantify numerical coupling error by reducing the coupling step. Then separate parameter uncertainty from climate or forcing uncertainty. A robust optimization should report a Pareto or regret surface across plausible environments, not one optimum at a nominal climate. If a learned closure is added, test whether it changes the inferred mechanistic parameters and whether it remains bounded under climates withheld from training. Case synthesis 3: stochastic gene expression. Use the same reaction network under CTMC/SSA, tau-leaping, and diffusion approximations. Choose observables that expose where the approximations disagree: low-copy-number distributions, first-passage times, or burst statistics rather than only the mean trajectory. Add a measurement model and compare filter innovations. For likelihood-free inference, use simulation-based calibration on synthetic draws before applying the posterior estimator to the observed experiment. The final portfolio is an evidence portfolio, not a feature catalogue. 27.1 Portfolio synthesis: four products, one scientific identity The portfolio is not seven unrelated repositories. Build four products that expose complementary evidence. NumeriCore demonstrates numerical verification and reusable scientific APIs. MultiScaleTwin demonstrates mechanistic modelling, inference, uncertainty and control. HybridSciML/BioScaleML demonstrates real-data ML and mechanistic–ML integration. Each product should reach the same release standard: a scientific contract, tests that target scientific invariants, an executable experiment, a diagnostic figure that could falsify the claim, provenance, CI, and a short technical defense. The defense is not a presentation of features. It answers: what is the scientific question, what assumptions make the computation meaningful, what evidence would make you reject the result, and what is the strongest limitation you would state to a reviewer or hiring panel? 27.2 One portfolio lifecycle, instantiated four ways A portfolio becomes coherent when every project answers the same sequence of professional questions with different scientific content. Do not maintain a separate milestone vocabulary for every repository. Use one lifecycle: 1. Claim: define the scientific or engineering claim and its scope boundary. 2. Reference: implement the simplest trustworthy baseline and verify it on a case with known 309

Evidence: add the diagnostic that could falsify the claim—convergence, profile likelihood, grouped validation, calibration, retrieval recall, or another method-specific test. Ç 4. Stress: inject a failure or distribution shift deliberately and show that the system detects it. 5. Engineering: expose the workflow through tested interfaces, configuration, provenance and CI. 6. Release: archive a reproducible experiment, limitations statement, citation metadata and technical defense. This lifecycle is the bridge between the book and the repositories. The repositories may contain more detailed issue lists, but they should never become a second curriculum. 27.2.1 Track A: NumeriCore—numerical trust The product claim is that a small set of numerical routines can be used through a stable API while exposing enough diagnostics to judge whether the computation is trustworthy. The scientific evidence is solver convergence, comparison against reference solutions, invariants, sensitivity to discretization, and explicit failure on inadmissible problems. A useful release contains at least one sparse linear workflow and one ODE workflow, each with a reference problem and a failure demonstration. Performance work is accepted only when numerical behavior is preserved to a stated tolerance. 27.2.2 Track B: MultiScaleTwin—mechanism, inference and decisions This track carries one mechanistic system through the entire evidence chain: model contract, solver verification, parameter identifiability, uncertainty, state estimation, and a decision such as robust design or control. The strongest version uses the same system across chapters rather than replacing it with a new toy at every stage. A digital twin claim is not earned by a live plot. It requires an observation model, synchronization with data, uncertainty or innovation diagnostics, and a documented rule for when the twin should not be trusted. 27.2.3 Track C: HybridSciML/BioScaleML—learning without losing scientific meaning Treat these two repositories as one portfolio track if both are retained. BioScaleML supplies the real-data discipline: grouped or nested validation, calibration, missingness/batch reasoning, and a simple statistical baseline. HybridSciML supplies the mechanistic interface: differentiable simulation, a named learned component, constraints, trajectory-level validation, and OOD/intervention tests. The portfolio story is stronger when the real-data model motivates a mechanistic question and the mechanistic model states what evidence would be needed to move from association to explanation. 27.2.4 Track D: ModelAgent—bounded scientific AI The product claim is not “an AI assistant for science.” It is a bounded evidence system in which retrieval, numerical tools, generation and provenance are separately measurable. Establish retrieval metrics before generation. Use typed tools whose inputs and outputs can be validated. Store source identifiers and tool traces. Add abstention or escalation when required evidence is absent. Evaluate on held-out questions and adversarial cases, then state clearly which failures remain attributable to the underlying model rather than your orchestration layer. CHAPTER B Worked Resolutions: Scientific Python Flu- Ç ency These are walkthroughs, not answer keys. For every problem, compare your own diagnostic artifact before reading the resolution. PF.1 Parametrized scientific tests Step 1 - identify the experiment table. The two optimization algorithms are different experimental cases even if they share the same acceptance criterion. Write that table explicitly as (label, callable) pairs. Step 2 - parameterize the test. 1 from functools import partial 2 import numpy as np 3 import pytest 4 5 @pytest.mark.parametrize( 6 "label,solver", 7 [ 8 ("local", solve_rosenbrock_local), 9 ("global", partial(solve_rosenbrock_global, seed=3)), 10 ], 11 ) 12 def test_rosenbrock_finds_reference_minimum(label, solver): 13 result = solver() 14 assert result.success, f"{label} solver did not converge" 15 assert np.linalg.norm(result.x - np.ones(2)) < 2e-3 16 assert result.fun < 1e-8 Step 3 - create a fresh fixture. 1 @pytest.fixture 2 def tumor_params() -> Params: 3 return Params(v=1.8, omega=0.9) The fixture function is called separately for each dependent test. If the object were mutable, one test would still not contaminate another. Step 4 - inspect the report. Run pytest -q -vv. You should see separate node IDs for the local and global cases. That independent reporting is the evidence that the refactor improved diagnosis rather than merely changed syntax. Common failure. Parametrizing only the expected number while still calling both solvers inside the test preserves the original diagnostic problem. Parametrize the actual changing experimental factor. 333

PF.4 Vectorized sweep Let k_t.shape == (P,), u.shape == (M,), and tumor.shape == (M,). The target output has shape (P, M). Step 1 - create broadcast-compatible shapes. k_t[:, None] has shape (P, 1); u[None, :] and tumor[None, :] have shape (1, M). Step 2 - compute. 1 kill = -k_t[:, None] * u[None, :] * tumor[None, :] 2 assert kill.shape == (len(k_t), len(u)) Step 3 - verify against the obvious implementation. 1 reference = np.empty((len(k_t), len(u))) 2 for i, value in enumerate(k_t): 3 reference[i] = -value * u * tumor 4 assert np.allclose(kill, reference) Step 4 - inspect memory cost. Broadcasting avoids the Python loop but still materializes the (P, M) output. Vectorization is not free memory. For extremely large P and M, chunking may be the better design. PF.5 Type the numerical boundary Step 1 - reproduce the checker limitation. NumPy stubs may infer a broader scalar/array type than NDArray[np.float64] for a linear solve. Step 2 - establish the runtime fact. 1 solution = np.linalg.solve(A, b) 2 if solution.dtype != np.float64: 3 raise TypeError("expected float64 solution") 4 return cast(FloatArray, solution) Step 3 - explain the cast in words. The cast is justified because the function constructs A and b from float64 arrays and checks the returned dtype before asserting the narrower static type. Common failure. Writing result: FloatArray = np.linalg.solve(...) is not a conversion; the checker will still compare the inferred and declared types. Scientific Modelling, AI & Research Software Engineering ○

CHAPTER D Final competence standard Ç The final standard is not the number of algorithms remembered. It is the ability to enter an unfamiliar scientific problem and construct a defensible chain: expose assumptions, choose a representation, verify the computation, connect observations to latent quantities, construct an inference or learning protocol, quantify uncertainty, design diagnostics that can falsify the pipeline, engineer the work as maintainable software, and state precisely what the evidence does and does not support. 341
